original.requirement:
## Problem

Allow independent change-harness runs to progress concurrently without weakening any existing correctness, independent verification, recovery or publication guarantees. Quality takes priority over elapsed time. Shared resources may serialize; **unattended operation, durable waiting and automatic resumption are required**. Ordinary contention must not become a failed run, an approval question or an abandoned task.

This request arose when implementation of https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/issues/10 could not start because https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/issues/39 already occupied the harness's one active slot. This issue requests an implementation of safe concurrent runs; the research below is design input, not proof that such support exists today.

## What is actually shared today

Source reviewed at [`796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf`](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/tree/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf), the target `master` revision during research on 28 October 2026.

- [`harness_state.py`](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/blob/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf/.agents/skills/implement-change-harness/scripts/harness_state.py): `repository_lock()` uses a short-lived, nonblocking POSIX `flock` under the common Git directory. This is a local mutex, not a remote lease or a lock held throughout test execution.
- The same helper stores one `active.json` in one orphan `harness-artifacts` branch. `initialize` rejects another active root/run; `validate_run_records` treats another unfinished run as invalid. This **logical singleton is persisted remotely** and follows clones to other machines.
- Checkpoints use expected-old local ref updates and normal non-force remote pushes. `artifact_sync` requires exact-tip confirmation and preserves competing histories. `remote_history` deliberately refuses adoption of changed run-state bytes. Those protections detect competing writers; they do not schedule independent writers or combine concurrent state changes.
- Different machines ordinarily eliminate conflicts over local Steam installations, local files and local GPUs. They still share GitHub task identity, PR operations and the remote artifact namespace. Shared mounts, remote test services or the same Steam/account data can also cross machine boundaries. Separate machines therefore need independent run records even when no hardware mutex is shared.
- Worktrees help with source isolation; they do not give each run a private repository configuration, shared refs, operating-system environment or physical device.

Removing the single-active assertion alone, using another clone, or giving each run a differently named local lock is insufficient.

## Research: interference classes and mitigations

### 1. Git state, artifacts, task identity and integration

[Git worktree documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree) describes private HEAD/index state alongside shared refs and default configuration; it also cautions about incomplete submodule support. Give each run/worker its own checkout, branch or detached candidate, build tree, scratch space and output namespace. Avoid concurrent writes to shared Git config, common dependency checkouts or a mutable installed harness package; pin the helper/schema and tool identities for each run.

Independent machines still contend on the current artifact ref. [Git ref updates](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-ref) support expected-old checks locally; [normal push rules](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-push) reject divergent updates. Neither is a distributed execution mutex. Options worth evaluating:

- Per-run orphan artifact refs, each with one canonical owner and exact-tip publication, plus a narrowly coordinated discovery/task-claim index. Use a ref namespace compatible with the existing `harness-artifacts` ref (a ref cannot also be a directory prefix).
- A single publication service that serializes short, validated transactions for multiple explicitly addressed runs in the existing branch.
- A transaction protocol that safely rebases **disjoint** run updates after rereading canonical state, without replaying external effects or merging conflicting state blindly.

Prefer the simplest design that meets the tests. Do not implement an automatic Git merge of arbitrary state JSON. Specify crash recovery, historical discovery, migration, owner takeover and exact publication semantics for the chosen layout. Global history validation must not be weakened to make contention disappear.

Claim the same canonical issue/deliverable at the correct repository-wide scope, including cross-machine starts and overlapping root/sub-issue runs. Different issues may run concurrently; two owners must not independently publish competing implementations of the same deliverable. Native dependency requirements remain authoritative. Material issue edits or target-base advances still invalidate affected approval tuples. Coordinate merge/wrap-up and branch cleanup with https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/issues/39; a completed run must not clear another run's active entry, approvals or queued work. No merge authorization is implied by this issue.

### 2. Fixed names, writable files, caches and test schedulers

[`fossilize_test.cpp`](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/blob/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf/test/fossilize_test.cpp) creates/deletes fixed relative filenames such as `.__test_tmp.foz`. [`test/CMakeLists.txt`](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/blob/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf/test/CMakeLists.txt) supplies build-relative layer output; [`layer_test.cpp`](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/blob/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf/test/layer_test.cpp) removes a dump-prefix glob. Different worktrees are insufficient if workers reuse a build/test directory. Use run/attempt-specific writable roots and immutable copied/read-only fixtures; resolve symlinks/aliases when identifying a shared resource. Cleanup must be restricted to owned paths, never broad user/global caches.

CTest offers [`RESOURCE_LOCK`](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/prop_test/RESOURCE_LOCK.html), [`RUN_SERIAL`](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/prop_test/RUN_SERIAL.html) and [resource allocation](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/manual/ctest.1.html#resource-allocation). These are useful within a CTest scheduler. **Design inference:** independently launched CTest processes need an additional shared authority; their in-memory schedules are not a host-wide lock. Resource allocation is not activated merely by declaring `RESOURCE_GROUPS`: it needs a resource specification and test-side selection. Missing prerequisites or missing allocation must never be counted as a passing required gate.

[The Mesa environment reference](https://docs.mesa3d.org/envvars.html) documents explicit shader-cache placement and XDG/home defaults. Give cache experiments private, proven cache locations for the actual driver/runtime, preserving the intended cold/warm sequence. Do not disable caching as a concurrency workaround when cache reuse is what the test verifies. Do not assume an OpenGL cache setting isolates every Vulkan/Steam/vendor cache.

### 3. Steam, game sessions and physical GPUs

The existing [verification guide](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/blob/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf/local-docs/verification.md) already requires baseline/candidate/restored-cache/warm-repeat phases, actual executable provenance, client/replay shutdown, original preservation and rollback. It warns against heavy device stress alongside a game. [`validate_roundtrip_sandbox.sh`](https://github.com/robinwassen/Fossilize/blob/796bba75ab32c13e1b50ee01fd7d067f17112cdf/cli/validate_roundtrip_sandbox.sh) deletes home-level driver caches and fixed `/tmp/gears.*.foz`; it must not become an unattended concurrent test unchanged.

Treat a real Steam experiment as an **exclusive transaction across setup, all comparison phases, descendants, restoration and rollback verification**, not just a lock around launching `steam`. Canonical resource identity should include the host/installation/account/library or prefix actually touched, plus the relevant physical GPU. Different AppIDs are not evidence of isolation. A private output directory does not isolate client restart, launch settings, installed executable replacement, driver cache priming, user session, saved games or shared service state.

[Valve describes the Steam Runtime](https://github.com/ValveSoftware/steam-runtime) primarily as a compatibility environment, including namespace-based containers. That is not a documented guarantee of independent Steam clients, cache state or GPUs. Do not claim containers or private HOME variables prove Steam isolation. Separate test users/VMs/hosts may provide stronger boundaries, but shared physical hardware or account/library state must still be inventoried and verified.

Conservatively serialize real GPU/cache tests on the same device until concurrency is specifically supported. Performance, timeout-sensitive and cold/warm comparisons need an appropriate quiet reservation against competing CPU/I/O/GPU work, not merely separate file paths. Device-reset/hang injection can require host-level exclusivity or a dedicated worker machine. Never launch destructive fault experiments on a normal shared desktop simply because other harness workers obey a mutex.

### 4. Locks, process lifetime and abandoned work

[Linux `flock`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/flock.2.html) is generally advisory: all participating launchers must cooperate. Lock descriptors refer to open file descriptions and can be shared across fork/dup; release behavior must be intentional. A lock inside a repository cannot coordinate another clone testing the same host resource. Use a stable host-wide authority for host resources and repository-wide authority for remote/task effects. Never unlink a live lock file or reclaim solely because a PID disappeared or a lease clock expired.

[Distributed-lock analysis](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html) explains how an expired lease owner can resume and write stale data. Use ownership generations/fencing at services that can validate them. Steam and a physical GPU cannot generally reject an arbitrary stale client's token: retain/quarantine their reservation until the old execution is confirmed stopped and restoration is established. Heartbeats and timestamps alone do not prove that.

The process completing a test can spawn grandchildren, daemonize or delegate to an existing service. Terminating only the shell is insufficient.
